title: Aphasia in Stroke and Neuroinfection
subject: Medicine
summary: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain injury, most often acute stroke in the dominant hemisphere. Recognise patterns, stage severity, and identify treatable causes common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Aphasia is loss of language function (speech, comprehension, reading, writing) due to cortical or subcortical damage, usually in the left (dominant) hemisphere.
b: Diagnosed clinically with bedside language tests (e.g., bedside naming, repetition, comprehension).
Imaging (CT/MRI) confirms lesion location; if unavailable, use clinical localisation.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB) or the Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination; in low‑resource settings use the simple 3‑point scale: mild, moderate, severe.
b: Mild: able to communicate basic needs, some errors.
Moderate: limited spontaneous speech, good comprehension.
Severe: minimal speech, poor comprehension, may need augmentative communication.

sections.p: In East African hospitals the common aetiologies are:
b: Ischaemic stroke (MCA territory) – most frequent.
Hemorrhagic stroke – intracerebral bleed in basal ganglia or lobar.
TB meningitis or tuberculoma affecting language cortex.
Cerebral malaria with focal infarcts.
HIV‑related opportunistic infections (CMV, toxoplasmosis).
Severe hypertension crisis causing watershed infarcts.
Broca’s (frontal) – non‑fluent, effortful speech, good comprehension, poor repetition.
Wernicke’s (temporal) – fluent but nonsensical speech, poor comprehension, impaired repetition.
Global – severe deficits in both production and comprehension.
Conduction – good comprehension, poor repetition, relatively preserved fluency.

t.b: Is there acute haemorrhage or large infarct? – Positive bleed directs to neurosurgical care; negative supports ischaemic stroke.
Identify early infarction, demyelination, or tuberculoma – guides specific therapy.

t.a: Blood glucose, full blood count, HIV test
t.b: Rule out metabolic contributors and identify HIV status for opportunistic infection risk.

t.a: Lumbar puncture (if meningitis suspected and CT safe)
t.b: Detect TB meningitis or cryptococcal infection – positive CSF guides antimicrobial therapy.
Assess for large‑vessel atherosclerosis – positive result may lead to secondary prevention.

sections.p: Unrecognised airway compromise from severe dysphagia, aspiration pneumonia, seizures, worsening neurological deficit, and malignant cerebral oedema.
b: Sudden deterioration in consciousness.
New focal weakness beyond the original area.
Fever or neck stiffness suggesting infection.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support language recovery and prevent complications.
b: Hemorrhagic stroke – control blood pressure, reverse coagulopathy, neurosurgical referral for evacuation.
TB meningitis – start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol plus dexamethasone; monitor liver function.
Cerebral malaria – give IV artesunate; treat seizures aggressively.
HIV opportunistic infection – start appropriate anti‑infective (e.g., pyrimethamine‑sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis) and optimise ART.
Speech‑language therapy – start within 48 h; use picture boards, simple phrases.
Swallowing assessment – bedside water swallow test; if unsafe, keep NPO and consider NG tube.

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on secondary stroke prevention and language rehabilitation.
b: Control hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidaemia.
Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) for non‑cardioembolic stroke.
Statin for all atherosclerotic stroke patients.
Regular speech‑therapy sessions, family‑led communication strategies.
Vaccination against meningitis and malaria prophylaxis where endemic.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic aphasia but have different pathophysiology.
b: Dysarthria – motor speech disorder with preserved language.
Global cognitive impairment – poor language due to dementia, not focal lesion.
Psychogenic mutism – voluntary silence without neurological deficit.
Normal CT early after ischaemia may miss infarct – repeat imaging if deficit persists.
CSF glucose may be normal in early TB meningitis; rely on cell count and protein.
Aphasia severity scores can be inflated if patient is fatigued or uncooperative.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive worsening of speech despite therapy
Signs of airway compromise or aspiration

faq.a: Spontaneous recovery occurs in the first weeks, especially in mild cases, but structured speech therapy markedly improves outcomes.

faq.q: Why is the left hemisphere dominant for language?
faq.a: In >90 % of right‑handed and many left‑handed individuals, language centres (Broca’s and Wernicke’s) are located in the left frontal and temporal lobes.

faq.q: Is aphasia a sign of stroke only?
faq.a: No; infections (TB, malaria), tumours, and traumatic brain injury can also cause aphasia.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with sudden non‑fluent speech and right‑hand weakness – what is the most likely vascular territory involved? — Left MCA territory; explains contralateral face‑arm‑leg weakness and Broca’s aphasia.
You have a patient with fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension – which cortical area is damaged? — Dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area).

A patient with HIV presents with aphasia and fever; CT is normal. What is your next diagnostic step? — Perform lumbar puncture (after CT rule‑out) to evaluate for TB meningitis or cryptococcal infection.

In a resource‑limited setting, CT is unavailable. How do you differentiate stroke from TB meningitis clinically? — Stroke: abrupt onset, focal deficit, no meningeal signs; TB meningitis: subacute onset, neck stiffness, fever, cranial nerve palsies.

Why is aspirin preferred over clopidogrel for secondary prevention in most African stroke patients? — Aspirin is cheaper, widely available, and has comparable efficacy; clopidogrel is reserved for aspirin intolerance.
A patient with severe aphasia cannot swallow. What immediate measure prevents aspiration? — Keep NPO, place NG tube for feeding, and arrange speech‑language assessment.
What feature distinguishes conduction aphasia from Broca’s aphasia? — Good fluency and comprehension with marked repetition difficulty in conduction aphasia; non‑fluent speech in Broca’s.

During rehabilitation, a patient’s comprehension improves but speech remains halting. Which therapy focus is most appropriate? — Intensive articulatory‑motor practice (speech‑production drills) alongside continued comprehension exercises.
